analysis.title: Breaking Beta
key_insights: 27% of large U.S. stocks had negative realized beta over the six months before September 30, 2026, versus a long-run average of 1.3%. NISA says this has no precedent in its large-cap record since 1990. The prior peak was 14% in November 2000 during the dot-com crash.

Six-month betas of five widely held U.S. low-volatility ETFs now range from -0.06 to 0.43, versus long-run averages of about 0.7 to 0.8. Two of the largest ETFs now behave as market-neutral. The change comes from a sharp fall in correlation with the market, not from a comparable fall in the funds' volatility relative to it.

The market is splitting between AI and most everything else. The ten largest U.S. stocks are 37% of index weight but 55% of MSCI USA index risk. Defensive sectors increasingly trade with negative correlation to the major index drivers.

In NISA's low-volatility proxy (100 lowest-volatility stocks, inverse-volatility weighted), negative-beta stocks are 61% of portfolio weight versus 26% for all large U.S. stocks. The negative-beta groups are utilities (beta -0.12), insurance (-0.15) and consumer staples (-0.17). Real estate is +0.02 and other is +0.12.

Annualized tracking error of the proxy, as a ratio to index volatility, has roughly doubled from its decade average, from about 0.7 to about 1.4 (1991-2023 average 0.55). NISA calls these strategies significant anti-AI allocations, with tracking error that may exceed index volatility itself.

Bringing the combined beta of the five ETFs to 1 with an index overlay requires 57% to 106% extra index exposure. Gross long exposure per dollar invested would be 206% (Invesco S&P 500 Low Volatility), 194% (SPDR US Large Cap Low Vol), 170% (iShares MSCI USA Min Vol), 169% (SPDR Russell 1000 Low Vol Focus) and 157% (Fidelity Low Vol Factor). Only 2000-01 came close historically.

An overlay sized on today's beta is a bet that correlation stays low. If fund betas return to their pre-2024 averages while overlays lag, combined betas would reach 1.4-1.7. A rebound like early 2020 would lift them to about 1.5-2.1.

An ex-ante overlay (set at month-end to one minus trailing six-month beta) delivered an average beta of about 0.85-0.95 over the past six months. The month-to-month spread of delivered beta widened from about 0.1-0.2 (2011-2023) to about 0.2-0.35, with monthly betas ranging from about 0.3 to 1.35 since April 2026.

Low-beta regimes have been persistent. Roughly 70-80% of a deviation from long-run beta remains after six months, implying a half-life of about 12-19 months. When the proxy beta last fell below 0.4, its average was 0.37 six months later and 0.35 twelve months later. The sample is only four episodes in 35 years.

The closest precedent is 2000-01. The proxy beta fell below 0.4 in April 2000, stayed there 18 months and bottomed at 0.14. Two years after the start it was still 0.46. The current episode has lasted 12 months (since October 2025), with beta now below zero (-0.07).

Medium-horizon (about 12-month half-life) statistical risk models have overstated U.S. portfolio market exposure over the past six months. Realized beta or shorter-horizon models have been more reliable, but they would imply substantial leverage today.

NISA's takeaways for low-volatility mandates: the allocation delivers less equity exposure than planned, benchmark-relative risk is up, a partial overlay sized between current and historical beta limits rebound overshoot, and portfolio construction (sector and risk controls, combining low volatility with other signals) is the main stabilizer. The five funds have lost between almost all and about half of their market exposure.

sector_views.rationale: Utilities in the low-volatility proxy have a six-month beta of -0.12 and trade against the main index drivers. NISA gives no rating.
Staples carry a beta of -0.17 in the low-volatility proxy. NISA describes the defensive group as negatively correlated with the AI-driven index leaders, with no rating.
Insurance carries a beta of -0.15 in the low-volatility proxy and is among the largest negative-beta holdings. NISA gives no rating.
Real estate has a beta of +0.02 in the low-volatility proxy, close to zero. NISA gives no rating.

risk_factors: Correlation renormalizing in a broad selloff or rebound would push overlaid low-volatility allocations to combined betas of 1.4-2.1, well above the target of 1.
Ex-ante overlays are unstable. Monthly delivered beta ranged from about 0.3 to 1.35 since April 2026.
Medium-horizon risk models have overstated market exposure over the past six months, while shorter-horizon models imply high leverage.
The historical sample is small: only four low-beta episodes in 35 years, two of them in the AI period.
Index concentration: AI leaders drive 55% of index risk from 37% of weight.
charts_described: Chart of the share of large U.S. stocks with negative six-month realized beta since 1990 shows 27% today versus a 14% peak in November 2000 and a 1.3% average.
Chart of trailing six-month betas of five U.S. low-volatility ETFs shows readings of -0.06, 0.06, 0.30, 0.31 and 0.43.
Chart of tracking error divided by index volatility shows 1.41 now versus a 1991-2023 average of 0.55 and a line at 1.0 where tracking error equals index volatility.
Chart of gross long exposure needed for beta 1 shows 206%, 194%, 170%, 169% and 157% for the five ETFs.
Chart of the proxy beta since 1990 shows beta of -0.07 now versus a 0.4 threshold, with the 2000-01 episode as the closest precedent.
vol_and_positioning: Low-volatility ETFs now hold far less market exposure than their mandates imply. Six-month betas are -0.06, 0.06, 0.30, 0.31 and 0.43 for the five funds, versus long-run averages of about 0.7-0.8.
Low-volatility tracking error is about 1.41 times index volatility, versus a 1991-2023 average of 0.55 and equality at 1.0.

Hedging a low-volatility allocation back to beta 1 takes up to about 206% gross long. This sets up a risk of overshooting if correlation normalizes, with combined betas reaching 1.4-2.1 in the rebound scenarios.
Concentration: the ten largest U.S. stocks are 37% of index weight and 55% of index risk.

tension_points.bull_case: An index overlay sized on current beta restores beta close to 1 and delivered an average beta of about 0.85-0.95 over the past six months, so the regime of low correlation can be hedged.
tension_points.bear_case: If correlation renormalizes, the overlay doubles market exposure and combined betas reach 1.4-2.1. Monthly delivered beta has also been unstable, ranging from about 0.3 to 1.35.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A rebound in correlation to the market, such as a return of fund betas to pre-2024 averages (combined beta 1.4-1.7) or a snap-back like early 2020 (about 1.5-2.1).

theme_stances.key_argument: Negative betas are extreme in breadth and duration, and low-volatility funds now act as hedges against the AI-driven part of the market.
theme_stances.evidence: The breadth of negative betas has no precedent
